– I appreciate that not all of these studies were available at the time of submission, but it could be helpful to update the discussion to also place the results in the context of more recent viral culture duration from serial swabbing data (Chu et al., JAMA Int Med 2022) and/or shedding profiles in human challenge data (Killingley et al., Nature Med 2022).

claims.claim: The generation-interval distribution plays a key role in determining the spread and control of emerging epidemics such as the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.
claims.source: The generation-interval distribution plays a key role in determining the spread and control of emerging epidemics such as the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the importance of generation-interval distribution in epidemiology, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: At the population level, the generation-interval distribution links incidence of infection, particularly the epidemic growth rate r, with the reproduction number R.
claims.source: At the population level, the generation-interval distribution links incidence of infection, particularly the epidemic growth rate r, with the reproduction number R (Gostic et al., 2020; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Gostic et al., 2020; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).

claims.claim: Short generation intervals, driven by pre-symptomatic transmission, have limited the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies for COVID-19, including contact tracing, case isolation, quarantine, and testing.
claims.source: In the case of COVID-19, short generation intervals, driven by pre-symptomatic transmission, have limited the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies, including contact tracing (Ferretti et al., 2020b), case isolation, quarantine (Sun et al., 2020), and testing (Grassly et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies examining mitigation strategies.

claims.claim: The generation- and serial-interval distributions can change over the course of an epidemic.
claims.source: The generation- and serial-interval distributions can change over the course of an epidemic.
claims.evidence: This is a general epidemiological principle supported by the subsequent explanation about mitigation measures.

claims.claim: Generation and serial intervals are affected by the behavior of the population and can be shortened by the introduction of mitigation steps such as social distancing and case isolation.
claims.source: For example, they are affected by the behavior of the population and can be shortened by the introduction of mitigation steps such as social distancing and case isolation, which limit the spread of the disease and reduce the probabilities of transmission after symptom onset (Ali et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ali et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The mean forward serial interval stayed constant until around January 17, 2020, and then decreased gradually.
claims.source: We found that the mean forward serial interval stayed constant until around the January 17, 2020, and then decreased gradually, indicating changes in transmission dynamics (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: A strict restriction on mobility (lockdown) imposed in Wuhan city on January 23 likely impacted generation and serial intervals of infectors who were infected a few days prior to this date.
claims.source: In particular, a strict restrictions on mobility (lockdown) imposed in Wuhan city on January 23 (Kraemer et al., 2020) likely impacted generation (and therefore serial) intervals of infectors who were infected a few days prior to this date – for example, an individual who developed symptoms on January 23 would have had reduced transmission after January 23, thereby shortening their generation and serial intervals.
claims.evidence: This claim combines a cited fact about the lockdown date with inference about its impact on transmission intervals.

claims.claim: The negative trend in the mean serial interval from January 17–18 onward matches the timing of the decrease in the effective reproduction number R(t) for domestic cases in Wuhan, China.
claims.source: The clear negative trend in the mean serial interval from January 17–18 onward also matches the timing of the decrease in the effective reproduction number R(t) for domestic cases in Wuhan, China, estimated by Lipsitch et al., 2020.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with estimates from Lipsitch et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The dataset used for estimating the unmitigated generation-interval distribution includes 77 transmission pairs with a mean serial interval of 9.1 days (95% CI: 7.9–10.2) and a standard deviation of 5.2 days.
claims.source: This dataset includes a total of 77 transmission pairs with a mean serial interval of 9.1 days (95% CI: 7.9–10.2), and a standard deviation of 5.2 days.
claims.evidence: This claim presents descriptive statistics from the curated dataset.

claims.claim: The unmitigated generation-interval distribution has a median of 7.9 days (95% CI: 6.8–9), a mean of 9.7 (95% CI: 8.3–11.2) days and standard deviation of 6.9 (95% CI: 4.3–10.1) days.
claims.source: We estimate that the unmitigated generation-interval distribution has a median of 7.9 days (95% CI: 6.8–9), a mean of 9.7 (95% CI: 8.3–11.2) days and standard deviation of 6.9 (95% CI: 4.3–10.1) days.
claims.evidence: This is the main result from the maximum likelihood analysis of the transmission pair data.

claims.claim: The correlation parameter between incubation period and generation interval is estimated to be 0.75 (95% CI: 0.5–0.9).
claims.source: Furthermore, we estimate a correlation parameter (see Methods) of 0.75 (95% CI: 0.5–0.9).
claims.evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the bivariate distribution analysis.

claims.claim: The estimated mean generation interval is longer than the observed mean serial interval (9.1 days) of the period in question.
claims.source: We note that our estimated mean generation interval is longer than the observed mean serial interval (9.1 days) of the period in question.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the estimated and observed values from the analysis.

claims.claim: During the exponential growth phase, the mean incubation period of the infectors is expected to be shorter than the mean incubation period of the infectee.
claims.source: During the exponential growth phase, the mean incubation period of the infectors is expected to be shorter than the mean incubation period of the infectee – this effect causes the mean forward serial interval to become longer than the mean forward generation interval of the cohorts that developed symptoms during the study period.
claims.evidence: This is based on theoretical understanding of epidemic dynamics and is supported by reference to Park et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Approximately 20% (95% CI: 6–32%) of total transmission occurs pre-symptomatically.
claims.source: The negative side of this distribution gives the pre-symptomatic transmission, which constitutes ≈20% (95% CI: 6–32%) of total transmission.
claims.evidence: This is derived from the inferred bivariate distribution of incubation period and generation interval.

claims.claim: The inferred generation-interval distribution has a heavier (right) tail compared to current available estimates.
claims.source: A comparison with the current available estimates of the generation-interval distribution (Ferretti et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020) reveals that the inferred distribution has a heavier (right) tail (Figure 4) and a higher median (7.9 days compared to 5.4–5.8 days) and standard deviation (6.9 days compared to 3.3–3.9 days).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous studies and visualization in Figure 4.

claims.claim: About 18.5% (95% CI of 10–25%) of the transmission occurs after 14 days in the unmitigated scenario.
claims.source: In contrast, our inferred generation-interval distribution predicts that about 18.5% (95% CI of 10–25%) of the transmission occurs after 14 days in the unmitigated scenario (assuming the behavior doesn't change due to quarantine, isolation, testing, etc.).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the inferred generation-interval distribution.

claims.claim: The distributions of Ferretti et al., He et al., and Sun et al. indicate a residual fraction of transmission after 14 days of 2–4%.
claims.source: The distributions of Ferretti et al., He et al., and Sun et al. indicate a residual fraction of transmission after 14 days of 2–4%, while the distribution assumed by Johansson et al. indicates only 0.2%.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with estimates from previous studies.

claims.claim: The bias in previous estimates likely reflects the effects of mitigation steps and changes in awareness-driven behavior that prevent transmission during late stages of infection.
claims.source: The bias in the previous estimates likely reflects the effects of mitigation steps, such as quarantine of exposed individuals, as well as changes in awareness-driven behavior, such as faster self-isolation after symptom onset, that prevent transmission during late stages of infection.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the causes of differences between the current study and previous estimates.

claims.claim: Using late cutoff dates, such as January 21, leads to similar underestimation as seen in previous sources.
claims.source: Our sensitivity analysis of the cutoff date for the period of unmitigated transmission indicates that using late cutoff dates, such as the January 21, leads to similar underestimation as seen in the previous sources.
claims.evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis presented in the study.

claims.claim: On average, only approximately 20% (6–32%) of the unmitigated transmission happens before symptoms appear.
claims.source: Our results suggest that, on average, only ≈20% (6–32%) of the unmitigated transmission happens before symptoms appear, lower than commonly stated values that already include mitigation effects (40–60% Ferretti et al., 2020a; Sun et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is derived from the bivariate distribution analysis and compared with previous estimates.

claims.claim: The basic reproduction number R0 is estimated to be 2.2 with a CI of 1.9–2.7.
claims.source: Combining our estimated generation-interval distribution with the early growth rate (Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007), we find R0 to be 2.2 with a CI of 1.9–2.7 (Appendix 1—figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is calculated by combining the generation-interval distribution with the growth rate using the Euler-Lotka equation.

claims.claim: The median generation interval of both the alpha and delta variants was estimated to be 6.7 days, 15% shorter than the original variant.
claims.source: The median generation interval of both the alpha and delta variants was estimated to be 6.7 days, 15% shorter than the original variant.
claims.evidence: This is an extrapolation based on viral kinetic information from Kissler et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The median generation interval of the omicron variant was estimated to be 5.8 days, approximately 30% shorter than the original variant.
claims.source: The median generation interval of the omicron variant was estimated to be 5.8 days, ≈30% shorter than the original variant.
claims.evidence: This is an extrapolation based on viral kinetic information from Hay et al., 2022.

claims.claim: More than 15–19% of the transmission potential occurs 5 days after symptoms for the three variants of concern in the absence of mitigation.
claims.source: Even though these generation intervals are considerably shorter than the 7.9 days median generation intervals of the wild type, there might be a considerable amount of late transmission – for example, we estimate that more than 15–19% of the transmission potential occurs 5 days after symptoms for the three variants of concern (VOCs), in the absence of mitigation.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the extrapolated generation-interval distributions for VOCs.

claims.claim: Individuals infected with the wild type still have, on average, approximately 18% of their transmission potential 14 days after infection.
claims.source: The tail of the survival function (Figure 4B) indicates that individuals infected with the wild type still have, on average, ≈18% of their transmission potential 14 days after infection.
claims.evidence: This is derived from the survival function of the generation-interval distribution shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: A strong correlation exists between the incubation period and the generation interval.
claims.source: We also found a strong correlation of the incubation period with the generation interval, accentuating the importance of quickly isolating individuals as soon as they show symptoms.
claims.evidence: This is based on the estimated correlation parameter of 0.75 from the bivariate distribution analysis.

claims.claim: The analysis by Johansson et al., 2021 underestimates the residual transmission after 10 days by an order of magnitude for the average individual (35% of the transmission vs. 4%).
claims.source: As can be seen in Figure 4B, our results suggest that this analysis underestimates the residual transmission after 10 days by an order of magnitude for the average individual (35% of the transmission vs. 4%).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's results and those of Johansson et al., 2021, based on Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Even when considering self-isolation of 70% of individuals immediately upon symptoms, there is a residual transmission of 11.8% compared to 1.3% in Johansson et al.'s estimates.
claims.source: However, even when considering self-isolation of 70% of individuals immediately upon symptoms, as Johansson et al., 2021 assumed in their analysis, we still find a residual transmission of 11.8% compared to 1.3% in Johansson et al.'s estimates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is calculated based on the generation-interval distribution and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The basic reproduction number R0 estimates derived in this study are close to reported values from early in the epidemic.
claims.source: The basic reproduction number R0 estimates derived here are close to reported values from early in the epidemic value (Chinazzi et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020b), despite the longer estimate for the generation-interval distribution.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with R0 estimates from previous studies.

claims.claim: The general shapes of the mean viral load trajectories and culture positivity, based on longitudinal studies, are comparable with the estimated unmitigated infectiousness profile.
claims.source: Indeed, the general shapes of the mean viral load trajectories and culture positivity, based on longitudinal studies, are comparable with our estimated unmitigated infectiousness profile (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2, comparison with Chu et al., 2022 ; Killingley et al., 2022; Kissler et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with viral load data from other studies, shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The durations of infectiousness and incubation periods for the alpha and delta variants would be shorter by 15% relative to the original strain.
claims.source: One prediction of our extrapolation procedure is that the durations of infectiousness and incubation periods for the alpha and delta variants would be shorter by 15% relative to the original strain, which is supported by independent studies (Brandal et al., 2021Grant et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2021; Singanayagam et al., 2021; Hart et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the extrapolation method that is supported by citations to independent studies.

claims.claim: Data on serial intervals were gathered from twelve relevant datasets identified through literature survey.
claims.source: Twelve relevant datasets were identified: (Ali et al., 2020; Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020a; Xia et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhanwei et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes the data collection methodology with citations to all source datasets.

claims.claim: The combined dataset contained 2000 pairs, including duplicates.
claims.source: In total, the combined dataset contained 2000 pairs, including duplicates.
claims.evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the raw dataset before deduplication.

claims.claim: After removing duplicates, 1002 transmission pairs remained in the dataset.
claims.source: Lastly, we looked at the datasets not containing information regarding the sex and age of the cases (additional 406 pairs) and added to the dataset only pairs with symptom-onset dates that did not occur already in the first group (71 of the 406 cases were added, resulting in 1002 transmission pairs in total).
claims.evidence: This describes the final dataset size after the deduplication process.

claims.claim: The incubation period distribution was assumed to follow a lognormal distribution with a shape parameter of 0.53 and a scale parameter of 5.5 days.
claims.source: The incubation period distribution was assumed to follow a lognormal distribution with a shape parameter of 0.53 and a scale parameter of 5.5 days, following Xin et al., 2021.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological assumption based on a previous meta-analysis.

claims.claim: The daily growth rates in the early outbreak period in Wuhan and in the rest of China were estimated to be r=0.08 day⁻¹ and r=0.10 day⁻¹, respectively.
claims.source: The daily growth rates in the early outbreak period in Wuhan in particular and in the rest of China were estimated by another study (Tsang et al., 2020) to be r=0.08 day–1 and r=0.10 day–1 , respectively.
claims.evidence: This cites growth rate estimates from Tsang et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Most available estimates of the generation-interval distribution did not fully account for mitigation effects such as contact tracing and case isolation.
claims.source: Most available estimates of the generation-interval distribution addressed the effects of mitigation only in a limited manner, not fully accounting for steps such as contact tracing and case isolation (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies with citations.

claims.claim: The distribution of realized serial intervals depends on the rate of the spread of the disease as well as the direction from which they are measured.
claims.source: First, the distribution of realized serial intervals depends on the rate of the spread of the disease as well as the direction from which they are measured: either forward from a cohort of infectors who developed symptoms at the same time or backward from a cohort of infectees (Park et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological issue in serial interval estimation, supported by citation to Park et al., 2021.

claims.claim: When the incidence of infection is increasing, recently infected individuals represent a bigger fraction of the population and are over-represented in cohorts of individuals who develop symptoms on a given day.
claims.source: When the incidence of infection is increasing, recently infected individuals represent a bigger fraction of this population and thus are over-represented in this cohort.
claims.evidence: This explains a statistical bias that occurs during epidemic growth, based on epidemiological theory.

claims.claim: Most analyses of serial-interval distributions assume that the incubation periods of the infector and infectee follow the same distribution.
claims.source: However, most analyses of serial-interval distributions assume that the incubation periods of the infector and infectee follow the same distribution (Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020), and only a few studies partially account for this dynamical bias (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of methodological assumptions in previous studies with citations.

claims.claim: Incubation periods and temporal profile of infectiousness are likely to be correlated across infectors.
claims.source: Second, incubation periods and temporal profile of infectiousness are likely to be correlated across infectors – that is, individuals that show symptoms later or earlier are also more likely to infect others later or earlier, respectively.
claims.evidence: This describes an expected biological correlation that is a key consideration in the modeling approach.

claims.claim: Most available studies make strict assumptions on the relationship between the incubation period and the generation interval.
claims.source: Most available studies make strict assumptions on the relationship between the incubation period and the generation interval – either assuming that they are independent (Ferretti et al., 2020b; Ganyani et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020) or that the time from onset of symptoms to transmission (TOST) is independent of the incubation period (He et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of methodological assumptions in previous studies with citations.

claims.claim: Biases can arise from the data collection process, such as determining who infected whom based on symptom-onset dates, which can miss pre-symptomatic transmission.
claims.source: Finally, biases can arise from the data collection process. For example, determining who infected whom based on their symptom-onset dates can miss pre-symptomatic transmission.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential source of bias in transmission pair data collection.

claims.claim: Long serial intervals may represent multiple chains of transmissions where intermediate hosts were not correctly identified.
claims.source: Likewise, long serial intervals may represent multiple chains of transmissions where intermediate hosts were not correctly identified.
claims.evidence: This describes another potential source of bias in transmission pair data.

claims.claim: These biases can cause overestimation of the mean serial interval as well as the mean generation interval.
claims.source: These biases can cause overestimation of the mean serial interval as well as the mean generation interval.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the direction of bias from data collection issues.

claims.claim: The mean serial interval for the early period of the epidemic was 7.8 days (95% CI: 7–8.6 days) according to Ali et al., 2020.
claims.source: Although this is substantially longer than the mean of 7.8 days (95% CI: 7–8.6 days) suggested by Ali et al., 2020, for the early period of the epidemic, there is considerable uncertainty in both estimates with overlapping CI.
claims.evidence: This cites a previous estimate from Ali et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Other studies that did not differentiate different stages of the epidemic estimated a much lower mean serial interval (4–6 days).
claims.source: Other studies that did not differentiate different stages of the epidemic estimated a much lower mean serial interval (4–6 days) (He et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhanwei et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This summarizes estimates from multiple previous studies with citations.

claims.claim: The incubation period distribution has a mean of 6.3 days and a standard deviation of 3.6 days according to Xin et al., 2021.
claims.source: We used the maximum likelihood framework to estimate the parameters of the joint bivariate distribution of the generation interval and the incubation period, assuming a known incubation period distribution (Xin et al., 2021) with a mean of 6.3 days and a standard deviation of 3.6 days.
claims.evidence: This cites the incubation period distribution parameters from Xin et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The model was able to fit the observed serial-interval data well with or without the growth rate adjustment.
claims.source: With or without the growth rate adjustment, the model was able to fit the observed serial-interval data well (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This describes the goodness of fit of the model, shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Changing the assumed growth rate during the early outbreak period had very little effect on the results.
claims.source: Changing the assumed growth rate during this period had very little effect on the results, with estimated mean increasing from 9.5 to 9.7 days, as assumed growth rates decreased from 0.16 to 0.04 day–1 (Appendix 1—figure 7).
claims.evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claims.claim: Changing the incubation period to one with a median in the range of 4–5.5 days had very little effect on the results.
claims.source: Changing the incubation period to one with a median in the range of 4–5.5 days (Appendix 1—figure 10), as well as inclusion of severe cases in the dataset (Appendix 1—figure 11) had very little effect.
claims.evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 10.

claims.claim: Inclusion of severe cases in the dataset had very little effect on the results.
claims.source: Changing the incubation period to one with a median in the range of 4–5.5 days (Appendix 1—figure 10), as well as inclusion of severe cases in the dataset (Appendix 1—figure 11) had very little effect.
claims.evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11.

claims.claim: Removing the transmission pairs with the highest serial intervals from the dataset caused a small decrease in the generation-interval distribution.
claims.source: The sensitivity analysis to high serial-interval values caused a slight decrease in the mean generation interval, but still resulted in a wide distribution. Removing the transmission pairs with the highest serial intervals from the dataset caused a small decrease in the generation-interval distribution.
claims.evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis.

claims.claim: For a removal of the top 10% values, the inferred distribution has a median of 7.2 days and a mean of 8.3 days.
claims.source: For a removal of the top 10% values, the inferred distribution has a median of 7.2 days and a mean of 8.3 days (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Switching the order of some of the transmission pairs caused a decrease in both the median and mean of the generation interval, as well as a decrease in the correlation parameter.
claims.source: Switching the order of some of the transmission pairs caused a decrease in both the median and mean of the generation interval, as well as a decrease in the correlation parameter (Figure 5G–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Even when reordering 10% of the pairs the distribution is wide, with the median of bootstrap estimates for the median generation interval being 7.2 days.
claims.source: However, even when reordering 10% of the pairs the distribution is wide: for example, the median of bootstrap estimates for the median generation interval is 7.2 days (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The unmitigated generation-interval distribution is likely wider than previously thought.
claims.source: These sensitivity analyses demonstrate the robustness of our conclusion: the unmitigated generation-interval distribution is likely wider than previously thought.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sensitivity analyses.

claims.claim: The cutoff date seems to be the dominant factor in the analysis, meaning that taking the effects of interventions into account is the most important for an accurate estimate of the generation-interval distribution.
claims.source: We conclude that the cutoff date seems to be the dominant factor in our analysis, presumably meaning that taking the effects of interventions into account is the most important for an accurate estimate of the generation-interval distribution.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different sensitivity analyses.

claims.claim: Superspreading likely had negligible effects on the analysis because the data included at most two events with more than two infectees (4 and 7).
claims.source: However, the data we chose to include in the analysis consisted of at most two events with more than two infectees (4 and 7), and therefore superspreading likely had negligible effects on our analysis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the dataset.

claims.claim: When mitigation strategies are introduced, the amount of post-symptomatic transmission is expected to decrease, leading to an increase in the fraction of pre-symptomatic transmission.
claims.source: When mitigation strategies are introduced, we would expect the amount of post-symptomatic transmission to decrease, leading to an increase in the fraction of pre-symptomatic transmission.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the effects of mitigation on transmission timing.

claims.claim: The estimate of the proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission is lower than previous estimates that looked at a later period.
claims.source: Thus, it is not surprising that our estimate of the proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission is lower than previous estimates that looked at a later period (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Sun et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous estimates with citations, explained by the timing of data collection.

claims.claim: The results match the trend shown by Sun et al., 2020, in which faster isolation of cases increases the pre-symptomatic fraction of transmission and shortens the mean generation interval.
claims.source: Furthermore, our results match the trend shown by Sun et al., 2020, in which the faster isolation of cases increases the pre-symptomatic fraction of transmission and shortens the mean generation interval.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with findings from Sun et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Both the bivariate lognormal model and the adjusted logistic TOST model estimate large means and standard deviations of the generation intervals, and a low proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission for the current dataset.
claims.source: Both models estimate large means and standard deviations of the generation intervals, and a low proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission for the current dataset.
claims.evidence: This describes results from comparing two different modeling approaches.

claims.claim: Applying both models to the data from Ferretti et al., 2020a, produced similar distributions with lower estimates for the mean generation interval and higher per-symptomatic proportion.
claims.source: Applying both models to the data from Ferretti et al., 2020a, produced similar distributions with lower estimates for the mean generation interval and higher per-symptomatic proportion (Appendix 1—figure 6).
claims.evidence: This describes results from applying the models to a different dataset, shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claims.claim: The results presented in this study are a product of the focus on the data prior to mitigation steps, in combination with the correction for the growth of the epidemic.
claims.source: This indicates that the results presented in this study are a product of the focus on the data prior to mitigation steps, in combination with the correction for the growth of the epidemic.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the key factors contributing to the study's findings.

claims.claim: Transmission pairs data can be prone to incorrect identification of transmission pairs, including the direction of transmission.
claims.source: Transmission pairs data can be prone to incorrect identification of transmission pairs, including the direction of transmission.
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation of the data type used in the study.

claims.claim: Pre-symptomatic transmission can cause infectors to develop symptoms after their infectees, making it difficult to identify who infected whom.
claims.source: In particular, pre-symptomatic transmission can cause infectors to develop symptoms after their infectees, making it difficult to identify who infected whom.
claims.evidence: This describes a specific challenge in identifying transmission pairs.

claims.claim: Data from the early outbreak might be sensitive to ascertainment and reporting biases which could lead to missing links in transmission pairs.
claims.source: Data from the early outbreak might also be sensitive to ascertainment and reporting biases which could lead to missing links in transmission pairs, causing serial intervals to appear longer (e.g., people who transmit asymptomatically might not be identified).
claims.evidence: This describes potential biases in early outbreak data.

claims.claim: When multiple potential infectors are present, an individual who developed symptoms close to when the infectee became infected is more likely to be identified as the infector.
claims.source: Moreover, when multiple potential infectors are present, an individual who developed symptoms close to when the infectee became infected is more likely to be identified as the infector.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential ascertainment bias in transmission pair identification.

claims.claim: These biases might increase the estimated correlation of the incubation period and the period of infectiousness.
claims.source: These biases might increase the estimated correlation of the incubation period and the period of infectiousness.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the potential effect of ascertainment biases on parameter estimates.

claims.claim: The relatively narrow ranges of uncertainty suggest that the results are not very sensitive to specific transmission pairs data points being included in the analysis.
claims.source: The relatively narrow ranges of uncertainty suggest that the results are not very sensitive to specific transmission pairs data points being included in the analysis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the bootstrapping results.

claims.claim: Although potential biases can decrease the inferred mean generation interval, the main conclusions about the long unmitigated generation intervals remained robust.
claims.source: The sensitivity analysis shows that although these potential biases can decrease the inferred mean generation interval, our main conclusions about the long unmitigated generation intervals (high median length and substantial residual transmission after 14 days) remained robust (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This summarizes the findings from sensitivity analyses shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: It is nearly impossible to find two completely unrelated datasets from the period prior to mitigation, limiting the ability of further validation of the current results.
claims.source: Due to the nature of early spread of a new unknown disease, it is nearly impossible to find two completely unrelated datasets from the period prior to mitigation, limiting the ability of further validation of the current results.
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation in validating the study's findings.

claims.claim: Without testing, the residual transmission after quarantine would be substantially higher than previous estimates suggest.
claims.source: Indeed, the unmitigated infectiousness profile suggests that without testing, the residual transmission after quarantine would be substantially higher – thus supporting the policy of requiring PCR or rapid tests for ending quarantines, as required in many countries.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about policy implications based on the estimated generation-interval distribution.

claims.claim: Quarantine and isolation measures typically begin several days after the infection event, suggesting that the actual amount of post-quarantine and isolation transmission would be lower than estimated.
claims.source: In addition, quarantine and isolation measures typically begin several days after the infection event, suggesting that the actual amount of post-quarantine and isolation transmission would be lower than what we estimate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the practical application of the estimates.

claims.claim: The R0 estimates are close to reported values from early in the epidemic despite the longer estimate for the generation-interval distribution, mainly due to using the corrected growth rate.

results.result: The authors identified January 17, 2020 as the cutoff date for unmitigated transmission in Wuhan by analyzing changes in forward serial intervals over time. The mean forward serial interval remained constant until around January 17, then decreased gradually, matching the timing of the Wuhan lockdown on January 23 and the decrease in effective reproduction number R(t). The curated dataset for the unmitigated period (up to January 17) contains 77 transmission pairs with a mean serial interval of 9.1 days (95% CI: 7.9–10.2).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 provide converging evidence for the January 17 cutoff date through temporal analysis of serial intervals (C6), mechanistic explanation linking the lockdown to transmission dynamics (C7), independent validation from R(t) estimates (C8), and descriptive statistics of the resulting dataset (C9). The approach is methodologically sound and the cutoff date is justified by multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Using maximum likelihood estimation on the curated early outbreak data, the authors estimated the unmitigated generation-interval distribution has a median of 7.9 days (95% CI: 6.8–9), mean of 9.7 days (95% CI: 8.3–11.2), and standard deviation of 6.9 days (95% CI: 4.3–10.1). The correlation parameter between incubation period and generation interval was estimated at 0.75 (95% CI: 0.5–0.9). Approximately 20% (95% CI: 6–32%) of transmission occurs pre-symptomatically. The estimated mean generation interval is longer than the observed mean serial interval (9.1 days), which is explained by epidemic growth dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 present the core quantitative findings from the bivariate lognormal model fitted to the data. The estimates are internally consistent, with appropriate uncertainty quantification via bootstrapping. The theoretical explanation for why the estimated generation interval exceeds the observed serial interval (C12-C13) is grounded in established epidemic theory (Park et al., 2021) and demonstrates methodological sophistication.

results.result: The inferred unmitigated generation-interval distribution has a heavier right tail compared to previous estimates (Ferretti et al., He et al., Sun et al.), with 18.5% (95% CI: 10–25%) of transmission occurring after 14 days versus 2–4% in previous studies. The authors attribute this difference to mitigation effects and behavioral changes in previous studies that were not fully accounted for. Sensitivity analysis confirms that using later cutoff dates (e.g., January 21) produces similar underestimation as seen in previous sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 provide a well-supported comparison with prior literature. The quantitative differences are substantial and clearly documented (C15-C17), the proposed explanation is plausible and mechanistically grounded (C18), and the sensitivity analysis (C19) directly tests the hypothesis that cutoff date selection drives the differences. The convergence of evidence strongly supports the conclusion that previous estimates were biased by mitigation effects.

results.result: The study estimates that only approximately 20% (6–32%) of unmitigated transmission occurs pre-symptomatically, which is lower than commonly stated values of 40–60% from previous studies that included mitigation effects. This difference is explained by the fact that mitigation strategies reduce post-symptomatic transmission, thereby increasing the relative fraction of pre-symptomatic transmission. The results are consistent with trends shown by Sun et al., 2020.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C60-C62 present a coherent argument about pre-symptomatic transmission that is well-supported by the data and theory. The lower estimate for unmitigated transmission (C20) is directly derived from the bivariate distribution analysis. The mechanistic explanation (C60) is logically sound, and the comparison with previous studies (C61-C62) provides external validation. The reasoning is internally consistent and theoretically grounded.

results.result: Extensive sensitivity analyses demonstrate the robustness of the main conclusions. The results were insensitive to variations in assumed growth rate (C50), incubation period distribution (C51), inclusion of severe cases (C52), and removal of high serial intervals (C53-C54). Switching the order of transmission pairs caused decreases in parameter estimates but the distribution remained wide even with 10% of pairs reordered (C55-C56). The cutoff date emerged as the dominant factor affecting the estimates (C58), confirming that accounting for intervention effects is most important for accurate estimation.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C58 document comprehensive sensitivity analyses that strengthen confidence in the main findings. The analyses systematically address multiple potential sources of bias and uncertainty. The conclusion that cutoff date is the dominant factor (C58) is well-supported by the comparative analysis across different sensitivity tests. The robustness of the wide distribution conclusion (C57) across multiple perturbations is particularly compelling.

results.result: The basic reproduction number R0 was estimated to be 2.2 (95% CI: 1.9–2.7) by combining the generation-interval distribution with early growth rates using the Euler-Lotka equation. This estimate is close to reported values from early in the epidemic despite the longer generation-interval distribution, primarily because the analysis used corrected (lower) growth rates from Tsang et al., 2020.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C29, C76 present a coherent analysis of R0 estimation. The methodology (Euler-Lotka equation) is standard and appropriate (C21). The comparison with previous estimates (C29) and the explanation for why the estimates are similar despite different generation intervals (C76) demonstrate good understanding of the interplay between generation interval and growth rate in determining R0. The reasoning is sound and well-documented.

results.result: The authors extrapolated unmitigated generation intervals for variants of concern (VOCs) by scaling the wild-type distribution based on viral clearance duration ratios from Kissler et al. and Hay et al. The median generation interval was estimated at 6.7 days (15% shorter) for alpha and delta variants, and 5.8 days (30% shorter) for omicron. Even with shorter intervals, substantial late transmission remains (>15–19% after 5 days post-symptoms). The extrapolation method assumes clearance duration differences reflect biological differences in infection rate, and is supported by qualitative similarity between viral load trajectories and transmission probability distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24, C31, C92-C98 describe an extrapolation approach with significant limitations acknowledged by the authors. While the methodology is clearly described and the assumptions are stated (C95-C96), the extrapolation relies on crude assumptions about the relationship between viral load kinetics and infectiousness (C77-C81, C86). The qualitative support from viral load trajectory shapes (C97-C98) is weak evidence for quantitative extrapolation. The validation from independent studies (C31) provides some support, but the overall uncertainty is high. The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations.

results.result: The study has important implications for quarantine and isolation policy. Individuals infected with wild-type SARS-CoV-2 retain approximately 18% of transmission potential 14 days after infection (C25). The strong correlation between incubation period and generation interval (0.75) emphasizes the importance of rapid isolation upon symptom onset (C26). The analysis suggests previous estimates (Johansson et al., 2021) underestimate residual transmission after 10 days by an order of magnitude (35% vs. 4%), and even with 70% self-isolation upon symptoms, residual transmission is 11.8% vs. 1.3% in previous estimates (C27-C28). These findings support policies requiring testing before ending quarantine (C74, C83), though actual post-quarantine transmission may be lower since measures typically begin days after infection (C75).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28, C74-C75, C83 present policy-relevant implications that follow logically from the main findings. The quantitative comparisons with Johansson et al. (C27-C28) are well-documented and striking. The policy recommendations (C74, C83) are appropriately cautious and acknowledge limitations (C75). However, the translation from unmitigated estimates to policy recommendations requires assumptions about real-world conditions that introduce uncertainty. The implications are reasonable but should be considered as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive policy guidance.

results.result: The authors assembled data from twelve datasets identified through literature survey, containing 2000 transmission pairs initially. After systematic deduplication based on infector/infectee IDs, sex, age, and symptom-onset dates, 1002 unique transmission pairs remained for analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 describe a systematic data collection and curation process. The methodology is clearly documented with specific steps for identifying and removing duplicates. The reduction from 2000 to 1002 pairs indicates substantial overlap across datasets, which the authors appropriately addressed. The approach is methodologically sound for aggregating data from multiple sources.

results.result: The analysis assumed a lognormal incubation period distribution with shape parameter 0.53 and scale parameter 5.5 days (mean 6.3 days, SD 3.6 days) from Xin et al., 2021 meta-analysis. Growth rates for early outbreak in Wuhan and mainland China were taken as r=0.08 day⁻¹ and r=0.10 day⁻¹ respectively from Tsang et al., 2020.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C48 document key methodological assumptions based on previous meta-analyses and studies. The choice to use established estimates from the literature is appropriate and well-justified. The Xin et al. meta-analysis is particularly relevant as it includes correction for growth rate effects. The sensitivity analyses (C50-C51) demonstrate these assumptions do not substantially affect the main conclusions.

results.result: The authors identify three major sources of bias in previous generation-interval estimates: (1) insufficient accounting for mitigation effects like contact tracing and case isolation (C37); (2) dynamical biases arising from epidemic growth that cause over-representation of recently infected individuals with short incubation periods in symptom-onset cohorts (C38-C40); and (3) correlation between incubation periods and infectiousness profiles that most studies assume to be independent or make strict assumptions about (C41-C42). Additional biases can arise from data collection, such as missing pre-symptomatic transmission or unidentified intermediate hosts (C43-C45).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 provide a comprehensive and well-articulated critique of methodological limitations in previous studies. The identification of these biases is grounded in epidemiological theory (particularly Park et al., 2021 for dynamical biases) and supported by citations to relevant literature. The explanations are clear and mechanistically sound. This critical assessment provides strong justification for the current study's methodological approach.

results.result: The bivariate lognormal model fitted the observed serial-interval data well with or without growth rate adjustment (C49). To test model sensitivity, the authors compared results with an alternative adjusted logistic TOST model from Ferretti et al. Both models produced similar results for the current dataset (large means/SDs, low pre-symptomatic fraction) and for the Ferretti et al. data (lower means, higher pre-symptomatic fraction), indicating results are driven by data selection (focus on pre-mitigation period) and epidemic growth correction rather than model choice (C63-C65).
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C63-C65 demonstrate appropriate model validation through goodness-of-fit assessment and comparison with alternative functional forms. The finding that different models produce similar results when applied to the same data, but different results when applied to different datasets, strongly supports the conclusion that data selection (particularly the cutoff date) is the key factor. This is excellent methodological practice that strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: The authors acknowledge several limitations of transmission pair data, including potential incorrect identification of transmission direction (C66-C67), ascertainment and reporting biases in early outbreak data (C68-C69), and potential inflation of estimated correlation parameters (C70). However, bootstrapping results show relatively narrow uncertainty ranges suggesting low sensitivity to specific data points (C71), and sensitivity analyses confirm main conclusions remain robust despite potential biases (C72). Superspreading had negligible effects as the dataset contained at most two events with >2 infectees (C59). Independent validation is limited by the impossibility of finding completely unrelated pre-mitigation datasets (C73).
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C66-C73 provide an honest and thorough discussion of limitations. The authors appropriately acknowledge potential biases (C66-C70) while also presenting evidence that these do not fundamentally undermine the main conclusions (C71-C72). The acknowledgment that independent validation is difficult (C73) is important context. The discussion of superspreading (C59) appropriately addresses a potential concern. This balanced treatment of limitations strengthens rather than weakens confidence in the work.

results.result: The authors compare their estimated infectiousness profile with viral load trajectories and culture positivity from longitudinal studies, finding qualitative similarity in general shapes (C30). However, they extensively discuss limitations of inferring infectiousness from viral load data: the relationship between viral load, culture positivity, symptom onset, and real-world infectivity is complex and not well characterized (C77); inference ability is particularly limited for late-stage infectiousness (C78); viral load models often miss later slow decay phases (C79); and individual-level variation is not captured in population-mean models (C80). Due to these limitations, the VOC extrapolation was restricted to a single clearance duration parameter (C81).
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C77-C81 demonstrate appropriate scientific caution regarding the use of viral load data. The authors acknowledge qualitative support (C30) while extensively documenting limitations (C77-C80) and adjusting their methodology accordingly (C81). This is exemplary scientific practice—using available data for qualitative validation while recognizing its limitations for quantitative inference. The conservative approach to VOC extrapolation is well-justified.

results.result: The authors discuss limitations and applications of their estimates. Studies of variant generation intervals are necessarily subject to behavioral and intervention effects (C82). Multiple biological factors beyond viral kinetics can affect infectiousness profiles (C84-C85). The extrapolations are necessarily crude (C86) and don't account for current interventions (C87), but can still be useful for assessing isolation and contact tracing measures (C88). The framework could be applied to future emerging strains (C89).
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C84-C89 provide appropriate context for interpreting and applying the results. The authors clearly delineate what their estimates do and do not capture (C86-C87), acknowledge additional complexity not addressed (C84-C85), and suggest appropriate applications (C88-C89). This demonstrates good scientific judgment about the scope and limitations of the work.

results.result: The authors conclude that their analysis provides a view of unmitigated infectiousness profiles that is a key ingredient for policy models (C90), and demonstrates the importance of considering biases in serial-interval data and underlying assumptions when estimating generation-interval distributions (C91).
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 appropriately summarize the main contributions of the work. The emphasis on unmitigated profiles as inputs for policy models (C90) correctly identifies the value proposition. The methodological lesson about considering biases (C91) is well-supported by the extensive sensitivity analyses and comparisons with previous studies throughout the paper.

results.result: The introduction establishes the importance of generation-interval distributions for understanding epidemic spread and control. Generation intervals link epidemic growth rate with reproduction number at the population level (C1-C2), and short generation intervals driven by pre-symptomatic transmission have limited mitigation strategy effectiveness for COVID-19 (C3). Generation and serial intervals can change during epidemics due to behavioral changes and mitigation measures (C4-C5).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide well-established background from epidemiological theory and previous COVID-19 studies. These are appropriately cited and serve to motivate the study. The claims are not novel findings but rather context-setting statements that are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: The observed mean serial interval of 9.1 days in the current study is compared with previous estimates: Ali et al. reported 7.8 days (95% CI: 7–8.6) for the early period with overlapping confidence intervals (C46), while other studies that did not differentiate epidemic stages estimated much lower values of 4–6 days (C47).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 provide appropriate context by comparing the observed serial interval with previous literature. The acknowledgment of overlapping confidence intervals with Ali et al. (C46) is scientifically honest, while the contrast with studies that didn't differentiate epidemic stages (C47) supports the importance of the temporal stratification approach used in the current study.
